## 1) Introduction
Crop production and harvest is an area of study whose output affects every general population. This is becuase everyone, regardless of their different facets of life - need to consume food to survive. With the growing trend of global temperature, food production and harvest quantity may fluctuate. 

This study aims answer question about the effects of heat treatment to cranberries and result we observe in production of cranberries. 

We aim of answer the following questions : 

1. How does heat stress affect yield as measured by the total weight of fruit? \n 
2. How does heat stress affect yield as measured by the total weight of healthy fruit? \n 
3. How does heat stress affect yield as measured by the percentage of healthy berries by count? \n 
4. How does heat stress affect yield as measured by the percentage of healthy fruit by weight? \n 
5. How do the cultivars, years, and intensity of the heat shocks (in the case of the acute heat stress experiment) affect the various measures of yield? \n

```{r, include=FALSE}
data_raw <- read.csv("acute_yield_data_fall_2026.csv")

data <- data_raw %>%
                mutate(
                  year = factor(year),
                  cultivar = factor(toupper(trimws(cultivar))),
                  intensity_group = factor(toupper(trimws(intensity_group)),
                               levels = c("D", "C", "B", "A")),
                  treatment = factor(toupper(trimws(treatment)),
                               levels = c("CONTROL", "OTC"),
                               labels = c("Control", "OTC")),
                  heat_group = factor(ifelse(treatment == "Control", "Control", as.character(intensity_group)),
                               levels = c("Control", "D", "C", "B", "A")),
                  pair_id = interaction(year, cultivar, intensity_group, plot, drop = TRUE),
                                total_weight = healthy_weight + rotten_weight,
                                healthy_count_pct = 100 * ( healthy_n / (healthy_n + rotten_n)),
                                healthy_weight_prop = (healthy_weight / total_weight),
                                healthy_weight_pct  = 100 * healthy_weight_prop,
                                pulses = as.numeric(c(A = 4, B = 3, C = 2, data = 1)[as.character(intensity_group)]))

```

  group_by(pair_id) %>%

            .groups = "drop") %>%
  pull(ok)))
stopifnot(all(data$total_weight > 0), all(data$healthy_n + data$rotten_n > 0))

# Part 2: within-pair_id log ratio OTC / Control
# Keep only the columns that are identical within a pair_id, plus the ones to spread.
# (Other columns such as rotten_n differ between the two rows and would prevent pivot_wider from merging the pair.)
pairs_wide <- data %>%
  select(pair_id, year, cultivar, intensity_group, pulses, treatment, healthy_weight) %>%
  pivot_wider(names_from = treatment, values_from = healthy_weight) %>%
  mutate(ratio = OTC / Control,
         log_ratio = log(ratio))

pairs_wide %>%
  group_by(year, cultivar, intensity_group) %>%
  summarise(n = n(),
            mean_log_ratio = mean(log_ratio),
            geo_mean_ratio = exp(mean_log_ratio),
            .groups = "drop")
#  %>%
  #print(n = Inf)

```{r, echo=FALSE}


# Part 3: log transform
grp <- data %>%
  group_by(year, cultivar, heat_group) %>%
  summarise(mean_raw = mean(healthy_weight),
            sd_raw   = sd(healthy_weight),
            mean_log = mean(log(healthy_weight)),
            sd_log   = sd(log(healthy_weight)),
            .groups = "drop")

# Put both scales in one long data frame (raw panel first, log panel second)
grp_long <- bind_rows(
  grp %>% transmute(scale = "Raw scale", year, cultivar, heat_group,
                    m = mean_raw, s = sd_raw),
  grp %>% transmute(scale = "Log scale", year, cultivar, heat_group,
                    m = mean_log, s = sd_log)
) %>%
  mutate(scale = factor(scale, levels = c("Raw scale", "Log scale")))

ggplot(grp_long, aes(x = m, y = s)) +
  geom_point(aes(shape = cultivar,
                 colour = ifelse(heat_group == "Control", "Control", "OTC")),
             size = 2.3) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", formula = y ~ x, se = FALSE,
              colour = "grey50", linewidth = 0.6) +
  facet_wrap(~ scale, scales = "free") +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(Control = "grey20", OTC = "tomato")) +
  labs(x = "Group mean", y = "Group SD",
       title = "Group SD versus group mean on the raw and log scale",
       subtitle = "Each point is one cultivar x year x heat group (20 points)",
       shape = "Cultivar", colour = "Treatment") +
  theme_bw(base_size = 11)

# Numerical version of the same question

#grp %>%
#  summarise(cor_raw = cor(mean_raw, sd_raw, method = "spearman"),
#            cor_log = cor(mean_log, sd_log, method = "spearman"))

```

The relationship between group means and standard deviations was examined on both the original and logarithmic scales to assess potential mean-dependent variability. On the original scale, a positive association was observed between group means and standard deviations, suggesting that variability increased with average healthy fruit weight. Following logarithmic transformation, this relationship became substantially weaker, indicating that the transformation may improve variance stability. Therefore, a log transformation was considered as a potential approach for addressing heteroscedasticity in subsequent statistical modeling.

Log transformations fix right-skewness—they cannot fix bimodality


```{r design-residuals, fig.width=9, fig.height=4.5, fig.cap="Absolute residuals vs fitted values from a Gaussian model. The raw scale shows a mild increase in spread with the fitted value; the log scale is flatter. This supports modelling log(total weight).", echo=FALSE}
m_raw <- lm(total_weight ~ heat_group * year + cultivar, data = data)
m_log <- lm(log(total_weight) ~ heat_group * year + cultivar, data = data)

bind_rows(
  data.frame(fitted = fitted(m_raw), abs_resid = abs(resid(m_raw)),
             scale = "Raw scale"),
  data.frame(fitted = fitted(m_log), abs_resid = abs(resid(m_log)),
             scale = "Log scale")
) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = fitted, y = abs_resid)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.6) +
  geom_smooth(method = "loess", se = FALSE, colour = "tomato") +
  facet_wrap(~ scale, scales = "free") +
  labs(x = "Fitted value", y = "|Residual|",
       title = "Absolute residuals vs fitted values: raw vs log scale") +
  theme_bw(base_size = 11)

#####################################################################
#####################################################################


m_raw <- lm(total_weight ~ heat_group + year + cultivar, data = data)
m_log <- lm(log(total_weight) ~ heat_group + year + cultivar, data = data)
bind_rows(
  data.frame(fitted = fitted(m_raw), abs_resid = abs(resid(m_raw)),
             scale = "Raw scale"),
  data.frame(fitted = fitted(m_log), abs_resid = abs(resid(m_log)),
             scale = "Log scale")
) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = fitted, y = abs_resid)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.6) +
  geom_smooth(method = "loess", se = FALSE, colour = "tomato") +
  facet_wrap(~ scale, scales = "free") +
  labs(x = "Fitted value", y = "|Residual|",
       title = "Absolute residuals vs fitted values: raw vs log scale") +
  theme_bw(base_size = 11)

```

While log transformation was unable to address the bimodial nature of total weight distribution, it looks like it stabalizes variance.

The figures support the following model structure:

- **log(total_weight)** rather than raw weight: the response is positive, the
  effects are naturally multiplicative, and the log-scale residuals are more
  homogeneous.
- **(1 | pair_id)**: control and heat plots in the same pair_id are strongly
  correlated, so the pair_id must be a random effect.
- **heat_group × year**: the 2024 and 2025 profiles have different shapes,
  especially for MQ; ST is much lower in 2025.
- **year:cultivar**: 2025 ST is much lower than 2024 ST, a baseline shift that
  is not a heat effect.
- **heat_group × cultivar**: MQ and ST differ mainly in level; their heat
  profiles are similar enough that the interaction is tested but not obviously
  required.

The model-building section below fits the candidate models H0–H4 and compares
them with AIC and likelihood-ratio tests.

pair_id structure

```{r design-pairs, fig.width=6.5, fig.height=5, fig.cap="Control and heat total weights within the same pair_id are strongly correlated (r = 0.84). This supports the pair_id random intercept (1 | pair_id).", echo=FALSE}
pair_heat <- data %>%
  filter(treatment == "OTC") %>%
  select(pair_id, heat_group)

wide <- data %>%
  select(pair_id, treatment, total_weight) %>%
  pivot_wider(names_from = treatment, values_from = total_weight,
              id_cols = pair_id) %>%
  left_join(pair_heat, by = "pair_id")

cor_pair <- cor(wide$Control, wide$OTC)

ggplot(wide, aes(x = Control, y = OTC, colour = heat_group)) +
  geom_abline(slope = 1, intercept = 0, linetype = 2, colour = "grey40") +
  geom_point(size = 2, alpha = 0.85) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(data = "#fee5d9", C = "#fcae91",
                                 B = "#fb6a4a", A = "#cb181d")) +
  labs(x = "Control total weight (g)", y = "Heat total weight (g)",
       colour = "Heat group",
       title = sprintf("Within-pair_id correlation: r = %.2f", cor_pair)) +
  theme_bw(base_size = 11)
```

Because r=0.84 represents a strong positive correlation, plants in the same pair tend to naturally start or grow at similar sizes (likely due to shared microclimate, soil, or location).
Model Justification: This high correlation proves that observations within a pair are not independent.
Mixed Model Syntax: It validates using a mixed-effects model with a random intercept for pairs - lmer(total_weight ~ heat_group + (1 | pair_id))—to control for pair-level baseline differences and avoid artificially inflated sample sizes/p-values.



## 4) How does heat stress affect yield as measured by the total weight of fruit?

### 4.1 Candidate models

Total fruit weight is positive and right-skewed, so we model `log(total_weight)`.
The candidate fixed-effect structures are:

```{r}
fit_lmm <- function(form) lmer(form, data = data, REML = FALSE)

h0_total <- fit_lmm(log(total_weight) ~ heat_group + cultivar + year + year:cultivar + (1 | pair_id))

h1_total <- fit_lmm(log(total_weight) ~ heat_group * cultivar + year + year:cultivar + (1 | pair_id))

h2_total <- fit_lmm(log(total_weight) ~ heat_group * year + cultivar + year:cultivar + (1 | pair_id))

h3_total <- fit_lmm(log(total_weight) ~ heat_group * (cultivar + year) + year:cultivar + (1 | pair_id))

h4_total <- fit_lmm(log(total_weight) ~ treatment * intensity_group + cultivar + year + year:cultivar + (1 | pair_id))
```

```{r}
models_total <- list(
  H0 = h0_total,
  H1 = h1_total,
  H2 = h2_total,
  H3 = h3_total,
  H4 = h4_total
)

aic_tab <- data.frame(
  Model = names(models_total),
  df    = sapply(models_total, function(m) attr(logLik(m), "df")),
  AIC   = sapply(models_total, AIC)
) %>%
  mutate(dAIC = AIC - min(AIC))

kable(aic_tab, digits = 2, row.names = FALSE,
      caption = "AIC comparison for total weight (ML fits).")
```

H2 has the smallest AIC, so we select H2.

### 4.2 Heteroscedastic residual variance

H2 assumes a common residual variance. Control and heat plots may differ in
their residual spread, so we refit the same fixed and random effects with
`nlme::lme` and allow a separate residual variance for Control and OTC:

```{r}
h2_lmm <- lmer(log(total_weight) ~ heat_group * year + cultivar + year:cultivar +
                 (1 | pair_id), data = data, REML = TRUE)



h2_hom <- lme(log(total_weight) ~ heat_group * year + cultivar + year:cultivar,
              random = ~ 1 | pair_id, data = data, method = "REML")
h2_het <- update(h2_hom, weights = varIdent(form = ~ 1 | treatment))

anova(h2_hom, h2_het)
```

The likelihood-ratio test is significant, so the model with
separate residual variances is preferred. We use `h2_het` for the final
estimates.


### 4.3 Coefficients of the final model

```{r}
coef_tab <- summary(h2_het)$tTable
coef_ci  <- intervals(h2_het, which = "fixed")$fixed

data.frame(
  Term       = rownames(coef_tab),
  Estimate   = coef_tab[, "Value"],
  SE         = coef_tab[, "Std.Error"],
  p_value    = format.pval(coef_tab[, "p-value"], digits = 3, eps = 1e-4),
  Ratio      = exp(coef_tab[, "Value"]),
  Lower_95   = exp(coef_ci[, "lower"]),
  Upper_95   = exp(coef_ci[, "upper"]),
  row.names  = NULL
) %>%
  kable(digits = 3,
        caption = "Fixed-effect estimates of the final heteroscedastic H2 model.")
```

The reference levels are Control, 2024 and MQ. The `heat_group` coefficients
are log ratios relative to Control in 2024 for MQ; the `:year2025` terms add
the extra change in 2025; `cultivarST` is the ST/MQ baseline difference in
2024; `year2025:cultivarST` is the extra 2025 change for ST.



### 4.4 Answer

Heat stress lowers total fruit weight, but how big the drop is depends
on the year and on how many pulses the plants get. On average, the four heat
levels are about 11.5% lower than Control. The drop is smaller in 2024 (about
7.8%) and larger in 2025 (about 15.1%). In 2025, A is about 36.6% lower and B about 19.1% lower. Each pulse trend points are about −9% per pulse overall, but it is
weak in 2024 (−3%, p = 0.36) and strong in 2025 (−15%, p < 0.0001). We do not
see a heat × cultivar interaction for p=0.28; MQ and ST differ mostly in
baseline, and the 2025 ST baseline is much lower. We also let Control and OTC
have different residual variances; the LRT supports this, so we
use that model for the final estimates.

# 5) How does heat stress affect yield as measured by the total weight of healthy fruit?

```{r}
# Part 6: model comparison
fit_lmm <- function(form) lmer(form, data = data, REML = FALSE)

# no heat effect at all (baseline: cultivar x year only)
h_noheat <- fit_lmm(log(healthy_weight) ~ cultivar * year + (1 | pair_id))
# heat effect is the same in every cultivar-year
h0 <- fit_lmm(log(healthy_weight) ~ heat_group + cultivar + year + year:cultivar + (1 | pair_id))
# heat effect depends on cultivar
h1 <- fit_lmm(log(healthy_weight) ~ heat_group * cultivar + year + year:cultivar + (1 | pair_id))
# heat effect depends on year
h2 <- fit_lmm(log(healthy_weight) ~ heat_group * year + cultivar + year:cultivar + (1 | pair_id))
# heat effect depends on cultivar and on year, but no three-way interaction
h3 <- fit_lmm(log(healthy_weight) ~ heat_group * (cultivar + year) + year:cultivar + (1 | pair_id))
# full model: heat effect can differ in every cultivar-year
h_full <- fit_lmm(log(healthy_weight) ~ heat_group * cultivar * year + (1 | pair_id))

models <- list(h_noheat = h_noheat, h0 = h0, h1 = h1, h2 = h2, h3 = h3, h_full = h_full)
```


```{r}
# AIC / BIC table
aic_tab <- data.frame(
  model = names(models),
  df    = sapply(models, function(m) attr(logLik(m), "df")),
  AIC   = sapply(models, AIC),
  BIC   = sapply(models, BIC)
) %>%
  mutate(dAIC = AIC - min(AIC), dBIC = BIC - min(BIC))
print(aic_tab, row.names = FALSE)
```

# Part 7: Equal-variance model and diagnostics
h2_lmm <- lmer(log(healthy_weight) ~ heat_group * year + cultivar + year:cultivar +
                   (1 | pair_id), data = data, REML = TRUE)
isSingular(h2_lmm)

# Residual diagnostics for the equal-variance model
par(mfrow = c(1, 3))

# Residuals vs fitted values, coloured by treatment
plot(fitted(h2_lmm), resid(h2_lmm),
     col = ifelse(data$treatment == "OTC", "tomato", "grey30"), pch = 16,
     xlab = "Fitted value (log scale)", ylab = "Residual",
     main = "Residuals vs fitted")
abline(h = 0, lty = 2)
legend("topleft", legend = c("Control", "OTC"),
       col = c("grey30", "tomato"), pch = 16, bty = "n")

# Normal QQ plot of the residuals
qqnorm(resid(h2_lmm), main = "Normal QQ: residuals", pch = 16, col = "grey30")
qqline(resid(h2_lmm))

# Normal QQ plot of the estimated pair_id effects
re_pair <- ranef(h2_lmm)$pair_id[, 1]
qqnorm(re_pair, main = "Normal QQ: pair_id effects", pch = 16, col = "grey30")
qqline(re_pair)

par(mfrow = c(1, 1))

# Residual SD by treatment
data %>%
  mutate(r = resid(h2_lmm)) %>%
  group_by(treatment) %>%
  summarise(sd_resid = sd(r))

```
```{r}
# Part 8: Model with separate residual variances for Control and OTC
library(nlme)

# Same fixed and random effects as h2_lmm, refitted with nlme
h2_hom <- lme(log(healthy_weight) ~ heat_group * year + cultivar + year:cultivar,
              random = ~ 1 | pair_id, data = data, method = "REML")

# Control and OTC plots have separate residual variances
h2_het <- update(h2_hom, weights = varIdent(form = ~ 1 | treatment))

# Likelihood-ratio test for unequal residual variances
anova(h2_hom, h2_het)

# Estimated residual SD of Control, and ratio OTC SD / Control SD
sigma(h2_het)
coef(h2_het$modelStruct$varStruct, unconstrained = FALSE)
```


```{r}
# Diagnostics of the unequal-variance model, using Pearson residuals
r_pear <- resid(h2_het, type = "pearson")

par(mfrow = c(1, 3))
plot(fitted(h2_het), r_pear,
     col = ifelse(data$treatment == "OTC", "tomato", "grey30"), pch = 16,
     xlab = "Fitted value (log scale)", ylab = "Pearson residual",
     main = "Residuals vs fitted")
abline(h = 0, lty = 2)
legend("topleft", legend = c("Control", "OTC"),
       col = c("grey30", "tomato"), pch = 16, bty = "n")

qqnorm(r_pear, main = "Normal QQ: residuals", pch = 16, col = "grey30")
qqline(r_pear)

re_pair <- ranef(h2_het)[, 1]
qqnorm(re_pair, main = "Normal QQ: pair_id effects", pch = 16, col = "grey30")
qqline(re_pair)
par(mfrow = c(1, 1))

# Pearson residual SD by treatment
data %>%
  mutate(r = r_pear) %>%
  group_by(treatment) %>%
  summarise(sd_resid = sd(r))
```
```{r}
# Part 9: Final model
h2_final <- h2_het
```


$$
\log Y_i = \mu + \alpha_{g_i} + \beta_{t_i} + (\alpha\beta)_{g_i t_i}
+ \gamma_{c_i} + (\beta\gamma)_{t_i c_i} + b_{k(i)} + \varepsilon_i,
$$
$$
b_k \sim N(0, \sigma_b^2), \qquad
\varepsilon_i \sim N\!\left(0, \sigma^2_{\text{trt}(i)}\right), \quad
\text{trt}(i) \in \{\text{Control}, \text{OTC}\},
$$
```{r}
# Coefficients of the final model
coef_tab <- summary(h2_final)$tTable
coef_ci  <- intervals(h2_final, which = "fixed")$fixed

data.frame(term     = rownames(coef_tab),
           estimate = coef_tab[, "Value"],
           SE       = coef_tab[, "Std.Error"],
           df       = coef_tab[, "DF"],
           p        = coef_tab[, "p-value"],
           ratio    = exp(coef_tab[, "Value"]),
           lower_95 = exp(coef_ci[, "lower"]),
           upper_95 = exp(coef_ci[, "upper"]),
           row.names = NULL) %>%
  kable(digits = 3)
```
```{r}
# Variance components of the final model
vc <- VarCorr(h2_final)
sd_pair <- as.numeric(vc["(Intercept)", "StdDev"])
sd_ctrl <- sigma(h2_final)
sd_otc  <- sd_ctrl * coef(h2_final$modelStruct$varStruct, unconstrained = FALSE)[1]

# Correlation between the Control and OTC plot of the same pair_id
icc <- sd_pair^2 / sqrt((sd_pair^2 + sd_ctrl^2) * (sd_pair^2 + sd_otc^2))

data.frame(component = c("pair_id SD", "residual SD (Control)", "residual SD (OTC)",
                         "within-pair_id correlation"),
           value = c(sd_pair, sd_ctrl, sd_otc, icc))
```


```{r}
# Part 10: Tests and contrasts
joint_tests(h2_final)

emm_h <- emmeans(h2_final, ~ heat_group | year)
```

```{r}
# Each intensity vs Control within each year, Dunnett-adjusted, as ratios OTC / Control
ct <- contrast(emm_h, "trt.vs.ctrl", ref = "Control")
summary(ct, type = "response", infer = TRUE)
```


```{r}
# Average OTC effect over the four intensities within each year
ct_avg <- contrast(emm_h, list("OTC avg vs Control" = c(-1, 1/4, 1/4, 1/4, 1/4)))
summary(ct_avg, type = "response", infer = TRUE)
```


```{r}
# Dose response among the four OTC intensities within each year
emm_otc <- emmeans(h2_final, ~ heat_group | year,
                   at = list(heat_group = c("D", "C", "B", "A")))
contrast(emm_otc, "poly")
```

# Multiplicative change in healthy weight per additional heat pulse
slope <- contrast(emm_otc, list("per extra pulse" = c(-3, -1, 1, 3) / 10))
summary(slope, type = "response", infer = TRUE)

# Difference in the dose-response slope between years (exploratory)
pairs(slope, by = NULL)
```

summary(contrast(emm_all, list("OTC avg vs Control" = c(-1, 1/4, 1/4, 1/4, 1/4))),
        type = "response", infer = TRUE)

```{r}
# Part 12: Sensitivity to the most extreme plots
# Pearson residuals put Control and OTC plots on the same scale
data$r <- resid(h2_final, type = "pearson")
data %>%
  arrange(desc(abs(r))) %>%
  select(pair_id, year, cultivar, heat_group, healthy_weight, r) %>%
  head(6)

# The whole pairs of the 3 largest residuals are removed and the model is refitted
out_pairs <- data %>% arrange(desc(abs(r))) %>% slice(1:3) %>%
  pull(pair_id) %>% as.character() %>% unique()
d_sub <- data %>% filter(!pair_id %in% out_pairs) %>% droplevels()

h2_sub <- update(h2_final, data = d_sub)

emm_sub <- emmeans(h2_sub, ~ heat_group | year)
summary(contrast(emm_sub, "trt.vs.ctrl", ref = "Control"), type = "response", infer = TRUE)
summary(contrast(emm_sub, list("OTC avg vs Control" = c(-1, 1/4, 1/4, 1/4, 1/4))),
        type = "response", infer = TRUE)

emm_sub_otc <- emmeans(h2_sub, ~ heat_group | year,
                       at = list(heat_group = c("D", "C", "B", "A")))
summary(contrast(emm_sub_otc, list("per extra pulse" = c(-3, -1, 1, 3) / 10)),
        type = "response", infer = TRUE)

From the first anova, we show that there is strong evidence that the association between heat group and healthy fruit count depends on cultivar, year or their combination.
But when we add a 2 way interaction model, we see that 2 way interaction model does way better.

-- One important detail: because nbinom2 uses a log link, the coefficients are on the log expected-count scale. Exponentiating a coefficient gives a count ratio.


heat_groupD, pvalue ( 0.0576 ), About 15.8% fewer healthy fruits than Control; borderline evidence

percentages are calculated as (exp(beta) - 1 ) * 100

What the model concludes :
Healthy fruit counts differ across several heat groups relative to Control.
The heat-group effects for C and B differ between cultivars.
The A-versus-Control effect differs between years.
The cultivar difference changes substantially between years.

There is no statistically significant evidence that the full three-way interaction improves model fit (\(p=0.263\), from your earlier comparison).

```{r, echo=FALSE}
plot_heat_effects <- function(
  model,
  term_pattern = "^heat_group",
  group_map = c("A" = "4 Pulses (A)", "B" = "3 Pulses (B)", "C" = "2 Pulses (C)", "data" = "1 Pulse (data)"),
  group_order = c("4 Pulses (A)", "3 Pulses (B)", "2 Pulses (C)", "1 Pulse (data)"),
  unit = "g",
  title = "Impact of Heat Stress Pulses on Yield",
  subtitle = "Change relative to Control baseline (0)",
  xlab = "Yield Change relative to Control",
  ylab = "Heat Treatment Level",
  sig_color = "red",
  insig_color = "green",
  conf_level = 0.95
) {
  # 1. Extract t-table from model summary
  tab <- summary(model)$tTable
  heat_rows <- tab[grepl(term_pattern, rownames(tab)), , drop = FALSE]

  if (nrow(heat_rows) == 0) {
    stop("No coefficients matching pattern '", term_pattern, "' were found in the model.")
  }

  # 2. Extract clean group names (e.g., "A", "B", "C", "data") and map to display labels
  raw_levels <- sub(term_pattern, "", rownames(heat_rows))

  mapped_labels <- if (!is.null(group_map)) {
    ifelse(raw_levels %in% names(group_map), group_map[raw_levels], raw_levels)
  } else {
    raw_levels
  }

  alpha <- 1 - conf_level

  # 3. Build plotting data frame
  plot_data <- data.frame(
    group = mapped_labels,
    estimate = heat_rows[, "Value"],
    se = heat_rows[, "Std.Error"],
    df = heat_rows[, "DF"],
    p_val = heat_rows[, "p-value"]
  ) %>%
    mutate(
      lower = estimate - qt(1 - alpha / 2, df) * se,
      upper = estimate + qt(1 - alpha / 2, df) * se,
      group = factor(group, levels = group_order),
      sig = ifelse(p_val < 0.05, "p < 0.05 (Significant)", "p ≥ 0.05 (Not Significant)"),
      label_text = paste0(round(estimate, 1), if (nzchar(unit)) paste0(" ", unit) else "")
    )

  # 4. Compute dynamic x-axis limits to prevent text label clipping across different scale types
  x_min <- min(plot_data$lower, na.rm = TRUE)
  x_max <- max(plot_data$upper, na.rm = TRUE)
  x_range <- x_max - x_min

  x_lim_lower <- x_min - (x_range * 0.28)
  x_lim_upper <- max(10, x_max + (x_range * 0.1))

  # 5. Build plot
  ggplot(plot_data, aes(x = estimate, y = group, fill = sig)) +
    geom_vline(xintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", color = "gray40", linewidth = 0.8) +
    geom_col(width = 0.55, alpha = 0.85) +
    geom_errorbarh(aes(xmin = lower, xmax = upper), height = 0.2, color = "black", linewidth = 0.7) +
    geom_text(
      aes(x = lower - (x_range * 0.02), label = label_text),
      hjust = 1, vjust = 0.5, size = 4.5, fontface = "bold"
    ) +
    scale_fill_manual(values = c(
      "p < 0.05 (Significant)" = sig_color,
      "p ≥ 0.05 (Not Significant)" = insig_color
    )) +
    scale_x_continuous(limits = c(x_lim_lower, x_lim_upper)) +
    labs(
      title = title,
      subtitle = subtitle,
      x = if (nzchar(unit)) paste0(xlab, " (", unit, ")") else xlab,
      y = ylab,
      fill = "Significance"
    ) +
    theme_minimal(base_size = 14) +
    theme(
      plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 16),
      plot.subtitle = element_text(color = "gray30", margin = margin(b = 12)),
      panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
      panel.grid.major.y = element_blank(),
      legend.position = "bottom"
    )
}
